content: The quality of evidence regarding the accuracy of screening methods for tuberculosis (TB), as demonstrated in the GRADE tables, is rated as low to very low. Despite this, modeling results provide some guidance that may assist in selecting algorithms to rule out active TB in various settings. For example, chest radiography (CXR) screening demonstrates a high negative predictive value (NPV), particularly when any abnormality on the chest radiograph is considered. In contrast, symptom-based screening has lower sensitivity, leading to a lower NPV, and screening for any TB symptom also has lower specificity, resulting in a higher proportion of false-positive results. These false positives cannot be immediately started on latent TB infection (LTBI) treatment after screening. Adding symptom screening to CXR in a parallel algorithm slightly increases the NPV and reduces the already low number of false negatives. However, this approach also increases the number of false positives, which delays the initiation of LTBI treatment. When evaluating the ability to rule in LTBI and predict progression to active TB, 29 studies met inclusion criteria and provided sufficient data for effect measure estimation. The primary effect measure of interest was the incidence rate ratio, comparing TB incidence following a positive test result versus a negative test result. However, few studies reported person-years of follow-up for test positives and negatives. Most studies provided the number of incident TB cases among test positives and negatives, allowing for the calculation of risk ratios. The risk ratio is often reported as it is a more complete effect measure and serves as a proxy for the incidence rate ratio. When there is no loss to follow-up and both test positives and negatives are followed for the full study duration, the estimated risk ratio and incidence rate ratio yield identical results. However, differential loss to follow-up can lead to discrepancies between these estimates. The majority of studies (65%) were prospective cohort studies conducted in highor upper-middle-income countries with a TB prevalence of less than 100 per 100,000 population (72%). About half of the studies followed participants for an average of 20–35 months. Overall, the quality of evidence for all review outcomes was low to very low, primarily due to high risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision, and indirectness. Limitations of the systematic review include the small number of studies directly comparing the tuberculin skin test (TST) and interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA), heterogeneous study populations, and insufficient studies to fully explore the predictive utility of LTBI tests in subgroups. Pooled risk ratio estimates for TST did not differ significantly by TB incidence or income level. However, it is challenging to determine whether pooled estimates reflect true differences between tests or are influenced by the heterogeneity of study populations. Further analysis of eight studies directly comparing TST and IGRA in the same population (head-to-head analysis) showed overlapping and imprecise confidence intervals for both tests. Only three of these studies provided sufficient person-time data to calculate incidence rate ratios. There is little evidence to suggest that either TST or IGRA should be preferred over the other for assessing progression to TB disease, consistent with previous systematic reviews conducted for WHO guidelines. Insufficient data exist to determine whether the tests differ in predictive utility among specific high-risk subpopulations. A systematic review of 39 original articles critically appraised the cost-benefit and cost-effectiveness of LTBI screening and treatment. Outcomes included incremental cost per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) or life-year (LY) gained and incremental cost per TB case averted. Providing preventive therapy without LTBI screening for individuals with HIV was cost-effective or cost-saving compared to no treatment in resource-limited settings (e.g., Uganda, India, Zambia) and high-income countries (e.g., Italy). However, this strategy was not cost-effective for other populations, such as contacts of active TB cases or patients with systemic lupus erythematosus. In high TB incidence settings, screening without LTBI testing was the most cost-effective strategy for children aged 0–2 years and the preferred strategy for children aged 3–5 years who were household contacts of TB cases. The incremental cost-effectiveness of IGRAs compared to TSTs is influenced by the relative performance of diagnostic tests, with Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination reducing TST specificity and favoring IGRA-only strategies. Two-step strategies (IGRA following TST) were the most cost-effective in high-income countries and high-risk populations. TST-only strategies compared favorably with IGRA-based strategies in two U.S. studies, one assuming a low treatment completion rate and the other involving a low-risk population (U.S. military recruits) where all screening strategies were not cost-effective. In 13 studies expressing costs in U.S. dollars, the cost to rule out active TB in individuals eligible for LTBI preventive treatment (including chest radiographs, clinical evaluation, and liver function tests) ranged from $28 to $188. Most studies were conducted in highor upper-middle-income countries, with one exception in India. Regarding the accuracy of CXR in ruling out active TB among LTBI treatment candidates, studies showed limitations in design, with less than half of participants receiving the reference standard. Accuracy was calculated under the assumption that those not receiving the reference standard were cultureand/or smear-negative (no active TB). The study populations were not specifically selected as LTBI treatment candidates, and all studies were from high TB burden countries, limiting generalizability to low-burden settings. For symptom-based screening, less than 25% of participants received the reference standard, and accuracy was calculated under similar assumptions. Estimates for sensitivity and specificity were imprecise, with wide confidence intervals for false negatives and false positives. There is limited evidence to suggest that either TST or IGRA alone, or in combination with other proxies for LTBI, can best identify individuals at the highest risk of progression to active TB. In summary, both TST and IGRA can be used to test for LTBI, but IGRA should not replace TST in lowand middle-income countries due to cost and resource considerations. Chest radiography is recommended alongside symptom screening to rule out active TB before initiating LTBI treatment. Individuals with TB symptoms should undergo further investigation for active TB and other conditions.
